_comment: Expected patient-summary content per case. The notes are synthetic and were written for this corpus: they contain no patient data, no identifiers and nothing derived from a real record. Anything added here must meet the same standard - a public clinical corpus is the single most likely place for patient data to enter a repository, and there the mistake is unrecoverable.
_input: A summary case names SEVERAL notes, in order, because that is the shape of the call: a whole record assembled into ONE user message. The profile assembles them under [clinical.summaryAssembly] in pack.toml - per-note cap, running total, line format, note type - so any second runtime reading this pack builds byte-identical input. Grading a single note here would measure a call no application makes. THE TRUNCATION PATH IS NOW GRADED. It was a stated gap here for as long as the corpus was three short records: none of them reached `totalChars`, so no graded case ever handed a model a PREFIX of a record, and the assembler's truncation branch was covered by a unit test and by nothing that produced a number. sum-en-09-long-admission is six ward-round notes of a real-length admission; the assembler uses five of them and drops the sixth, and the case's answer key is written against what the model was actually GIVEN rather than against the complete record - which is the whole point, and is why `assembled.truncated` is recorded per case in the trace.
_matching: This task grades SET EXTRACTION over free text, so an expectation is a set of terms rather than a literal string: there is no single correct wording for 'type 2 diabetes diagnosed six years ago'. `match` is a list of ALTERNATIVES; each alternative is a list of terms that must ALL appear (case- and accent-insensitive substring) in SOME element of the model's array for that field. An item matches if ANY alternative matches. Both levels are load-bearing. The AND level: ['metformin','850'] matches 'metformin 850 mg twice daily' but not a bare 'metformin' the model guessed - and crucially a bare term would also match 'metformin stopped', the opposite fact. The OR level: a fact has more than one correct spelling, and scoring 'essential hypertension' as a MISS because the key said 'high blood pressure' is a scorer defect wearing a model result's clothing.

_expectKinds.present: Must appear in the named field. Counted in the gated recall denominator.
_expectKinds.absent: Must NOT appear in the named field. Catches the two failures worth catching: a fact filed in the wrong list (a completed study still listed as pending), and a fact invented outright. Each `absent` here names a specific trap the notes lay.
_expectKinds.empty: The whole field must be `[]`. Stronger than listing absents one by one, and it is what makes the thin-record case measurable: any content at all is an invention.

_floor: itemRecallFloor gates the eval: of `present` expectations, the share the model produced. Same asymmetry as the vital-signs task - a missed problem is invisible to the clinician while a spurious one is deleted in a click. It is set LOWER than the vital-signs floor (0.80 against 0.90) and that is a statement about the task rather than a concession to a model: keyword matching over paraphrase cannot be as sharp as comparing a transcribed number, so the same true performance scores lower here. A floor tuned until a particular model passed would be worthless; this one was chosen from what the task can resolve.

cases.name: sum-en-01-diabetes
cases.note: Three notes over a year, arranged so that reading only the first is wrong on three counts. Amlodipine is prescribed in note A, continued in note B and STOPPED in note C, so it belongs in no list; empagliflozin appears only in note B; the HbA1c requested in A is reported in B and therefore not pending, while a NEW HbA1c is requested in C and is. The father's bowel cancer in note C is family history and belongs nowhere. Discriminator: the record is read as a whole and the later notes correct the earlier ones.

cases.name: sum-es-02-epoc
cases.note: The same longitudinal shape in Spanish, with the drug traps that only an acute encounter produces. Metilprednisolona is ONE intravenous dose given in the emergency department and prednisona is a five-day course - neither is usual medication - while oxygen at 2 L/min is not a drug at all. The spirometry requested in note A is performed and reported in note C, so it is no longer pending; the cardiology assessment introduced in C is. Tiotropio appears only in the last note.

cases.name: sum-en-03-thin
cases.note: A healthy patient with a sprained ankle and nothing else: no regular medication, and by the second note nothing outstanding at all. This case grades one item and can otherwise only lose points - it is the summary task's equivalent of the note with no vital signs, and it measures whether a model handed a thin record fills the lists with the comorbidities and follow-ups such a record USUALLY carries. The paracetamol is the trap: bought over the counter, taken as required, and stopped after a week, in a record that twice states there is no regular medication.

cases.name: sum-en-04-heart-failure
cases.note: Three cardiology visits in which one drug is REPLACED rather than stopped: ramipril goes and sacubitril valsartan arrives in the same sentence of note B, so a model reading only for stop words keeps the wrong one. Furosemide is started in A and never mentioned as changed, which means it survives. The echocardiogram is requested in A and reported in B, and the cardiac rehabilitation is referred in B and completed in C, so both leave the pending list by the end - while the device assessment introduced in C is the only thing still outstanding. The father's myocardial infarction in C is family history and the note says so.

cases.name: sum-es-05-nefrologia
cases.note: Two nephrology visits in Spanish. The trap is a five-day course of prednisona given during a brief admission for gout, which is a finished course and not habitual medication - the same shape as the metilprednisolona trap in sum-es-02, in a different specialty and with a different drug, because one instance of a failure mode is an anecdote. Alopurinol's DOSE changes between the notes and the later one is the answer. The renal ultrasound is requested in A and reported in B, so it is no longer pending; the dialysis assessment requested in B is.

cases.name: sum-en-06-anticoagulation
cases.note: A record that ENDS EMPTY. Warfarin is stopped and edoxaban started in note B - a switch, not an addition - and the thyroid function requested in B is reported normal in C, after which the note says in words that nothing is outstanding and the patient is discharged. So `pending` must be [], on a record whose first two notes both contain pending items. It is the hardest shape in this task: a model that carries an earlier note's outstanding item forward is doing exactly what a summary is for, and here it is wrong.

cases.name: sum-en-07-oncology
cases.note: Surveillance after cancer surgery, where the pending list is the whole point of the record. Two investigations are requested in note A; one is performed and reported in note B and one is still not booked, and the note says which is which in plain words. Nothing about the medication changes, which is deliberate: this case tests one axis and is quiet on the others, so a failure here is unambiguous.

cases.name: sum-en-08-asthma
cases.note: An asthma review where the same drug appears in both notes at two DOSES and the later one is right, which is the dose analogue of the drug-stopped trap. Two courses of oral steroids are described as finished in A and again in B, so prednisolone belongs in no list. The spirometry requested in A is reported in B; the nitric oxide test introduced in B is the outstanding one.

cases.name: sum-en-09-long-admission
cases.note: THE TRUNCATION CASE, and it was named as a gap in this file before it was written: the other records run to about 1.5 kB, none of them reaches [clinical.summaryAssembly].totalChars, and no graded case exercised the path where a model is handed a PREFIX of a record. A six-note admission does. The sixth note is dropped by the assembler and the marker says so, which makes the answer key deliberately different from the one a complete record would produce: the pneumococcal vaccination is still outstanding at the end of note E and is given in note F, so `pending` must contain it. A model that somehow answered as though it had read note F would be scored WRONG, which is correct - it is being asked about the input it was given. The trace records `assembled.truncated` for exactly this reason, and this case is what makes that field mean something.

cases.name: sum-es-10-geriatria
cases.note: A polymedicated elderly record in Spanish with a withdrawal in the last note: donepezilo is stopped for intolerance and NOT replaced, so it belongs in no list, while hierro added in note B does. The social-work assessment requested in A is completed in B and the falls-unit referral requested in C is not, so the pending list turns over completely across three notes. The husband who attends the same clinic and has diabetes is the third-party trap - the note names him precisely so that a record built from this one cannot quietly acquire his diagnosis.
